title: Tired ad or slow starter: reading fatigue from history
hook: Tired ads and slow starters look the same on a cost chart.
caption:
Tired ads and slow starters look the same on a cost chart.
One needs a new opening. The other needs you to leave it alone.

Both show a cost per order above your account average, so the cost column cannot separate them.

History can. An ad can only be tired if it was once good.

In Galvor's analysis of video ads launched May to September 2026, some ad styles started about 35% dearer per order in their first two months and ended close to average over their life. Cut those in week one and you never see the second half.

Swipe for the order I check things in, and the four calls it leads to.

slides.headline: Tired ad or *slow starter*?
slides.sub: They look the same on a cost chart. Here is how I tell them apart.

slides.headline: Fatigue needs a *before*
slides.body:
An ad can only be tired if it was once good.

So the first check is history. Did this ad ever beat your account average for a couple of weeks?

If it never did, you are looking at something else.

slides.headline: Four signals, *read together*
items: Hook rate — falling while the cost of reach holds
Frequency — the same people, seeing it again
Hold rate — people stop, then leave sooner
Cost per order — the last one to move

slides.headline: dearer per order in the first two months, for *some ad styles*
slides.sub: They ended close to average over their life.
slides.source: Source: Galvor analysis · video ads launched May–Sep 2026

slides.headline: Scale, cut, *refresh*, test
items: Scale — still beating average, signals steady
Refresh — the message sells, the opening is tired
Cut — never was good, and is not improving
Test — too little delivery to judge yet

slides.headline: Read the history *before* the cost.
